speechtext: Upon his superannuation a civil servant is paid a superannuation allowance of a certain percentage of his salary based on the last three years of his service. Is it possible under the present act, in the event of a lower salary having been paid for one or more of the final years, for a civil servant to choose any three consecutive years of his service to form the basis of his superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Civil Service Superannuation Act (chapter 24, revised statutes, 1927) provides that superannuation allowance shall be based on the average salary of the contributor during the last five years or ten years of his service, depending upon which part of the act applies. The act further provides that in the case of a contributor to whom part III applies, that is, one who on July 19, 1924, was subject to the provisions of part I of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act, his allowance shall not be less than that to which he would have been entitled if he had continued to be subject to said part I of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act. Under the provisions of that act, the basis is the average yearly salary during the last three years of service. In no case is provision made for a civil servant to choose particular years for the purpose of determining the average salary to be used as a basis of superannuation allowance.

Questions
international joint commission
Does the government propose to reorganize the International Joint Waterways Commission in harmony with Canada's present status?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With permission of the house I should like to answer this question orally. The appointment and procedure of the International Joint Commission is at present in substantial harmony with Canada's national status. Article 7 of the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909, under which the commission was constituted, provides for the appointment of the Canadian members by " His Majesty on the recommendation of the Governor in Council of the Dominion of Canada." The governmental references to the commission are made by the Canadian government. I have used the words " in substantial harmony " for the reason that as a matter of fact there is the use in several places in the treaty itself of the terms " the United Kingdom" and "His Majesty's government" where if the treaty were now being drafted the term " His Majesty " would be used instead. In many articles of the treaty reference is made' direct to the government of the Dominion of Canada, but there are three instances in which it is ambiguous. When I give my hon. friend those instances he will see in a moment that any ambiguity has been removed by the understanding reached at the last Imperial conference. Article V of the treaty reads:
The United Kingdom, by the Dominion of Canada, or the province of Ontario, may authorize and permit, etc.-
The words " United Kingdom " would be out of place in any drafting of a treaty today between the United States and Canada, and it may be taken as now being the fact that the words "His Majesty" are the words that are signified in that particular.
Article VII reads as follows:
The high contracting parties agree to establish and maintain an International Joint Commission of the United States and Canada composed of six commissioners, three on the part of the United States appointed by the President thereof, and three on the part of the United Kingdom appointed by His Majesty on the recommendation of the Governor in Council of the Dominion of Canada.
In this section as will be seen the words " United Kingdom " occur again. If the treaty were being drafted to-day the words " United Kingdom " would not appear, but the words "His Miajesty" would appear instead.
Article X reads as follows:
Any questions or matters of differences . . . may be referred for decision to the International Joint Commission by the consent of the two parties, it being understood that on the part of the United States any such action will be by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and on the part of His Majesty's government with the consent of the Governor General in Council.
The words " on the part of His Majesty's government " would read to-day in a redrafting of the treaty " on the part of His Majesty."
I submit, however, that in view of the following statement which appears in the report of the Imperial conference of 1926, it is scarcely necessary to redraft the treaty in order to have it conform to the status of Canada as laid down at the last Imperial conference, although in some particulars this might be desirable:
We propose that it should be placed on record that, apart from provisions embodied in constitutions or in specific statutes expressly providing for reservation, it is recognized that it is the right of the government of each dominion to advise the crown in all matters relating to its own affairs. Consequently, it would not be in accordance with constitutional practice for advice to be tendered to His Majesty by His Majesty's government in Great Britain in any matter appertaining to the affairs of a dominion against the views of the government of that dominion.
So with respect to the International Joint Commission having regard to the procedure set forth at the last Imperial conference and the practice to be adopted in accordance with that procedure, any matter relating to the commission would be dealt with by His Majesty on the advice of his Canadian ministers. Wherever the treaty makes a reference to His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, it would be understood, in accordance with the practice as now laid down, that this would mean His Majesty's advisers in Canada in so far as the matters have to do with Canadian domestic or external affairs.
There is one point I should like to clear up because I have seen some mention in the press of an intention on the part of the government to make some alteration because of the change in Canada's status. There is no intention to make any changes. Some time before the last Imperial conference, a communication was sent to the British government asking their opinion as to whether, in the event of an appointment being recommended by His Majesty in council in Canada, the wording of the treaty which nominally places the appointment in the hands of His Majesty's government in Great Britain, would be construed as in any sense giving that apointment to His Majesty's government in Great Britain rather than to His Majesty's government in Canada. The reply which was received was to the effect that most
Privilege-Mr. Cahan

certainly the King would be advised in these matters by his Canadian ministers and not by his ministers in Great Britain. Since the Imperial conference with respect, for example, to exequaturs issued to consuls, the practice has been adopted of having them bear the signatures of His Majesty the King and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Canada where formerly they bore the signatures of His Majesty the King and the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in Great Britain. If to-morrow a commission were being issued to a new member of the International Joint Commission, it would be signed by His Majesty the King and would bear the signature as well of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Canada and not the signature of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in Great Britain as was formerly the case.

speechtext:
During my experience of public works administration in the province of New Brunswick, we imported a considerable quantity of this material1 for road purposes. We did not allow the contractors in road construction to use this chloride; it was used by the government, under rigid engineering supervision, for the purpose of laying the dust on gravelled roads and no other purpose. It was not used until after the road was finished and handed back to the province by the contractor. Then the patrol 56103-87
crews used the chloride on the road, and I understand it is being used in every other province of the Dominion. At any rate that is the way we used it, and I know it is the way it is being used to-day in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it used in solution?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: No, it is used in powder form. It is contained in tin or metal barrels containing about 300 pounds to the barrel. A barrel will cover a road 40 feet wide for a distance of about 200 feet. In some cases it is is distributed just as sand is distributed on icy streets in winter time, in other cases by machinery. The former plan is followed in New Brunswick. It is quite a help in preserving the road. May I say for the sake of information that when chloride is placed on the roads in the month of June no further application will be needed that year, and the following spring you can see the good effects of the material not only in keeping down the dust but in consolidating the gravel surface of the road.

That argument is something that I protest against, and I wish to protest strongly against this policy of destroying established industries. Let me read this extract from the Journal of Commerce of Canada :
The government have, therefore, decided to make free under all tariffs non-alcoholic preparations and chemicals for disinfecting, dipping and spraying.
As a result, the fruit growlers will be better able to import their insecticides for spraying and dusting instead of buying them as heretofore from such institutions as the Deloro Smelting and Refining Company of Deloro, Ontario, which uses the arsenic ores of Cobalt and other Canadian deposits and employs Canadian labour.
This company has spent much on research and made heavy investments in plant which undoubtedly would not have been made had they felt that their protection against imports would be any less than that enjoyed by the producer of these imports. In fact, it was the excellent work which this company did in research, working in conjunction with the mining school at Queen's University, in an effort to find new uses for cobalt and arsenic, that started the Canadian people to consider favourably the expenditure of public money in order to encourage such research.

As the representative of an industrial centre I again lodge my protest against the action of governments who will not for one moment consider the efforts that these men have put forth in order to establish their business, in order to employ men, men who come to a centre, buy homes, establish themselves and then wake up some morning after this parliament assembles to find that their industry is injured and possibly t'heir work brushed aside. We should at every opportunity, protest against this attitude of the government. As I understand the matter, the firuit growers appeared before the tariff board and asked for a seasonal protection against fruit being imported into Canada. The government of the day did not care to launch into a seasonal tariff, and probably with some justification, but something has to foe done for these men. When a government is without a policy, just dealing with individuals, each individual must be fixed up in some way or another. These gentlemen were sent home and told:	You cannot
get any protection on your fruit but we will tell you what we will do; we will allow you to have brought free into this country some of these non-alcoholic preparations or chemicals for disinfecting, dipping or spraying. I consider that is a wonderful gift to hand out to people who are endeavouring to have their industry protected. Regardless of the fact that there were in Canada industries employing men, the government was to penalize them in order to protect a few men by some such means. As long as an industry is affected and as long as these industries are being disturbed by the action of government, as a representative of an industrial centre I intend to protest against this kind of thing. In this country we need work and we need homes. We must protect in some way or another these people who have launched into an enterprise after years of research and they should not be disturbed in this way. I desire to protest against this proposed change in the tariff.

As representing a fruitgrowing constituency where the people desire and appreciate these changes very much, I should at least express the other side of the question. I do not know how many are employed in the industry about which my hon. friend has been speaking, and I do not know whether that industry will be injured or not. I rather fancy not, but I know that reductions of costs such as this to the fruit growers of eastern Canada are very important and will be greatly appreciated. The smelting people connected with the mining industry have been endeavouring to find some use for their arsenic and other by-products, and research work carried on by the Deloro Smelting Company has proven that arsenic, which is a product of many ores in this country, can' be used in this way. Arsenic is contained in a great many ores, and it is a problem to ascertain the best use that can be made of it, a problem upon which the mining industry has spent a great deal of money in research, and at their own expense. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The implication was absolute, and I say further that if the minister will study the question he will remove that discrimination against formaldehyde. If he is right in making free the sprays that remove an evil from fruit trees, then he must make this smut destroyer free. I know exactly what it is; I am only a lawyer but I have studied some of these problems. It has been my business to do so. And when members of this House of Commons get up and assert the right of their constituents to have this smut destroyer placed on the free list, and are told that had they supported the minister's budget they might have got it-to be told so by implication-it is an insult to the institution of parliament. I must say there is nothing more offensive.to parliamentary life than that gentlemen who represent rural constituencies, as these gentlemen do, should be told in this parliament, when they assert that this formaldehyde should be placed on the free list in order that they might use it for the purpose of destroying smut, their request might have been considered as was the request of the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), who voted for the budget. I say, this is not the way in which parliamentary institutions should be maintained; and I, as a member of this house, resent that sort of thing. It is subversive of parliamentary life and is injurious to the whole body politic. I resent it now and will continue to resent it. Gentlemen who loudly cheer observations of that kind are striking a fatal blow at the institutions of the country in which they live.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He did not sav that.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is within the memory of the members of the house. No.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is $175,000; so the return says.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: In wages?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Spent on the Rideau
canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, in wages and material.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Exactly; it does not
matter what the amount is. As my hon. friend knows, the labour involved is the kind

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of labour engaged in building concrete walls and digging trenches for the erection of them; and every year in connection with that work-
You are getting away from the item.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I am following the example of my hon. friend's leader, and a minister who is attacked in this manner surely has the right to reply. If I have not on this item I shall be glad to raise it as a matter of privilege, and we might consider a little what is called the freedom of parliament, about which we hear in some moving accents in this house. I will be very glad to bring down in this house the records of the work done on the Rideau and other canals by my predecessor in office and by my predecessors of the party to which my hon. friend belongs, and I can assure him that I have cleaned up a good many of these situations which they started at that time. I will be glad to advance proof of that statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Another covert insinuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, I do not make covert insinuations, nor do I put threats into the mouths of other people, but I do endeavour to sit quietly while other people are speaking. There are always hundreds of applications for casual labour of this character. Those who apply are required by the superintendent to be able-oodied and fit for the work in question, returned soldiers receiving the preference. They are supposed to be recommended by the sitting members for Ottawa. That has always been the case, and in that regard we have followed the practice which formerly existed. It does not do my hon. friend credit to make those statements; he knows very well that this has always been the practice. I would be very happy to have the whole situation left to the Civil Service Commission, and I am sure the members for Ottawa feel the same way about it. We would then be rid of that nuisance.

It is common talk around this city, and if it is not true it is doing a great injustice to the members who sit for Ottawa, that no man has an opportunity of getting work on that canal without going to those members. Not only that, but it is also common talk that every time a man or woman looks for work of that kind they are asked first as to their political affiliations, for whom they worked during the election and to what Liberal association they belong. I am not stating anything which is not common talk in Ottawa at this moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No officials of my department ask any such questions.
I am not saying anything about the officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The practice is that which has always been followed; work is given on recommendation of the members representing the city of Ottawa.

And the members representing this city look into their political affiliations. But I also wish to put myself on record as opposed to the attitude taken by any Minister of Finance who tells any party oi group in this house that if they would support him they might get what they ask for, and if they do not support him they will not get what they ask for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

The minister made this
statement, that if hon. gentlemen in that corner had supported his party, he would be much more inclined to listen to them. In other words, the budgets of this country are not drawn up for the purpose of doing good to the country as a whole, but are,drawn up for the purpose of doing good to the political party in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Do you think these budgets
are good for us?

They seem to be hoodwinking the people rather successfully, and by the last vote or two I must confess that the people seem to be carried away a little by them. Personally, however, I do not think they are good for the country, although they have helped or something has helped to keep this party in power for another short time. I wish to protest against that situation, because I do not think it is for the good of this country or for the good of any political party in this country in the long run to make changes in the tariff designed only to benefit a particular party. I believe the minister will agree with me, if he cares to express an opinion, when I say that changes in the tariff should be made for the benefit of the country as a whole rather than for the benefit of any political party, and they should not be determined by the support or non-support given the government by any political party or group in this house.

I want to say another word regarding this matter, and it is something I do not like to say. The minister has thrown down the gauntlet to us; to-day he has passed an insult on this little group and the great class we represent as having no voice here

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
and no right to a voice because we did not support the budget. The minister made that plain statement. The Minister of Finance not only confirmed what the Prime Minister said in the west during the last election campaign, but he has directly insulted this group of members. The Prime Minister said on the platform at Saskatoon during the last election that we could get anything if we would only join with the Liberal party. In his speech this year the Minister of Railways said we might have been co-operating with the Liberal party this year, and that we had thrown insults at those members who had seen fit to co-operate with that party. That is right, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is right.

The minister said we could
only secure what we wanted and could only make our plans effective by log-rolling and dealing.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No, no.

The words of the minister

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I did not use those words in the connection they are now being used by my hon. friend, and he knows that very well.

In connection with group
government, the minister said it could only be accomplished by log-rolling and dealing. The minister himself came into public life through the very organization which sent us here.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I should draw the attention of hon. members to the rule which states that discussion in committee must be directly relevant to the item or clause under discussion at that particular time. Hon. members know very well that for a considerable time the discussion has not been relevant to the matter before the committee. I would therefore ask hon. members to bring their remarks more closely to bear on the item now before us.

This is a direct discrimination between two classes of primary producers, and that is why I protest against it. I also protest against the words of the minister as an insult to us and to our whole class.
What is the item before the committee?

I rise to a question of
privilege. It has pleased the distinguished leader of the opposition to make statements in which he has mentioned the members for

the city of Ottawa. I want' to say to the hon. gentleman in the most courteous manner possible, but at the same time in the most vehement and effective way, that the statement he has made with reference to the securing of work on the Rideau canal is not at all warranted by the facts. The appointments have been made not only on the recommendations of the hon. members for the city of Ottawa; but they have been made on the recommendations of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fontaine); of the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Perras); of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Goulet), and on the recommendations of other hon. members for adjoining constituencies.
The hon. member for Carleton?

Not the hon. member
for Carleton (Mr. Garland), I am happy to say. For those appointments I take the responsibility. No man was asked at any time to pay a dollar to join any Liberal association in order to secure work.
It is more than it is worth.

When my hon. friend
gets into power he can ask $5. Now I say again it is not true that those appointments were made in that way; they were made as the Minister of Railways has said. If I were to produce a list of those who have been appointed to work on the Rideau canal you would find a large percentage of returned soldiers who were unable to do that hard, arduous work under those difficult conditions, and in addition you would find that both myself and my colleague sitting for this city had received recommendations from the Salvation Army, from the ministers of different churches, from priests, from the welfare bureau and from other charitable institutions, and that those were given the preference. In conclusion may I ask my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) if he has ever given any position within his power to a Grit since he has been in charge of any operations of the Ontario Liquor Commission?

I can assure my hon.
friend any way that we have never demanded any fee from applicants or asked them to produce a certificate from the Conservative association before they got the positions.

I was just wondering what
this question of privilege has to do with the matter before the committee. Any question of privilege should have some relation to the matter under discussion.

I rise to a
point of order. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) said that I could approve of the way they were appointing men to work on the Rideau canal in the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No. If that is my hon. friend's point of order I can assure him it is not well taken. I would not expect him to approve of that. What I said-and he can rise to a point of order afterwards if he likes-was that he could confirm the statement that this system has been in operation ever since confederation.

All I have
to say is that I cannot confirm it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I see.

When this
Rideau canal retaining wall was built during the Conservative regime, the money was apportioned to three parties, the federal, government, the provincial government, and the corporation of the city of Ottawa. It was done as an unemployment measure, and no letters were required from one party any more than the other. At that time the Conservative party was in power and my county got its share. All I have to say with regard to the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chev-rier) is that he is really beside the mark in the assertions he has made here to-day, and I hope that if he has any respect for himself he will apologize for some of the statements he has made. speechtext: What my hon. friend has said is correct.
That may be so, but the minister should know that neither threats nor anything else are going to divert me from doing what I believe to be right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I should like to have
said a *word upon the item before it was

passed. speechtext:
No, this has been before the
department for, I think, two or three years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is only one point
I desire to make clear about that. It will certainly prevent the development of the industry in this country, and there is just this to be said with respect to all these matters: The Minister of Finance has had to meet this difficulty and I suggest to him it is desirable to overcome it. When you say that goods shall be free only if utilized in a certain way and at a particular point, the great difficulty has 'been in knowing that they are used for that purpose and at that point, and usually what has happened is that advantage has been taken of that particular provision of the tariff item to enable the goods that are thus free from tariff to be used for purposes not intended. Therefore I suggest to the minister

that as far as possible he should not use those words, that is, fix the application of the exemption by specifying the use of the article imported and the place at which it may be utilized.

Customs tariff-438. Locomotives and motor cars for railways and tramways, and chassis, tops, wheels and bodies for same, n.o.p.: British preferential tariff, 22i per cent; intermediate tariff, 30 per cent; general tariff, 35 per cent.

I should like on this item to draw the attention of the minister to what I consider an injustice in the way of carrying out, probably by regulations which have been referred to, a previous item on this subject. While I am on my feet I should like to express my appreciation of item 438e, which provides for a reduction of duty on cars for mining. This will help the coal mining industry, and I wish to draw the minister's attention to a somewhat similar case. In 1924 a reduction was made in the duty on machinery for sawing lumber and so on. The item concludes something like this:
Machinery, logging cars, block and tackle and complete parts thereof for logging purposes exel usi vely.
It was the government's policy at that time to reduce the cost of production in the basic industries, and it appears to have been worked out by regulations in a way that in some degree more or less prevented the advantage being obtained. Apparently by regulations it was held that, as regards locomotives, the line on which these locomotives ran must be exclusively on land belonging to a logging company. I have in mind a logging company which has forty miles of well ballasted railway nearly all on its own land, but because there is half a mile of other property between it and the shore to which the logs go, these locomotives were held not to come within the scope of this clause. Another objection that was made is this. It was held that if a logging car was used for ballasting this railroad- and this is a road on which nothing would ever travel except logs-therefore the cars could not be held to come under this item. I would suggest that if a logging car is used
for hauling logs three hundred days in the year and used for only a couple of weeks to ballast the line, it should be allowed to come under the item. Another objection made presumably by regulation was that the locomotive must be only on the side line-what is called yarding, I believe-hauling logs out of the bush on to the branch line. If the locomotive went on the main line, they would not allow any reduction on it. I object to this because nothing is carried over this line except logs and perhaps the stores going up for the various camps. I would ask if the minister's attention could not be attracted to a better definition of that item which is or used to be, 453e. It would carry out the absolute purpose for which it was passed and be of considerable help to the lumbering industry generally.

I notice that
item 438 of the old tariff has been repealed and item 438 of the new tariff covers locomotives and motor cars used on railways, but there is no provision for automobiles or vehicles of all kinds which stood in the old item. Where do they come in now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only change in this item is the addition of the letters " n.o.p.".

The old item
438 read:
Locomotives and motor cars for railways and tramways and automobiles and motor vehicles of all kinds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend must have an old tariff. That is not the last one.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

I approve of this change; it is a good measure of improvement for conditions in the mining industry, but I am a little at a loss to know why automatic carloaders were not included. I think an application was made to the board for the inclusion of automatic carloaders in any reduction. None of these is made in Canada; no industry in this country would be harmed in the least, and it is very unlikely that any of these will ever be made in Canada as the consumption is very small.

speechtext: My hon. friend will be pleased to know that upon representations made to me by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, he will find an item covering that a little further on. I have an amendment to provide for that.

I am delighted to know that representations from that side of the house have been influential for once. They do not seem to have been so before. I made representations to that effect twelve months ago and I presume they have had some weight with the minister. I thank him very heartily.
The hon. gentleman flatters himself too much.

I cannot let this
item pass without taking an opposite view to that held by a good many members in this house, because at the present time the manufacture of locomotives and other equipment used for mining is now being started in Canada. If hon. members who are speaking for the coal industry will kindly remember that their coal will be used in Ontario only in manufacturing plants, they will realize that this item and the reductions made in this way will not encourage the use of western coal.

The hon.

Should we not make sure that we can rely upon the domestic factories for the production of certain kinds of machinery indispensable to our industrial life? This is a matter which I think might very well engage the attention of some of my hon. friends during the recess. They might consider the principle laid down by Adam Smith in the early part of his great work, as to the desirability of a country being always in a position to protect itself in matters such as this-using the word protection in a sense different from that implied in relation to tariff questions. Should we not put ourselves in a position where we could be independent of the outside world in this regard? I submit that the minister should study this question from every angle to determine whether or not, in a new country with a limited population and vast undeveloped resources, it is wise for us to leave ourselves dependent upon producers outside Canada, sometimes three thousand miles away. prevent evasion of the law. In reality, as far as I understand this particular part of the cotton schedule, it is a reclassification for administrative purposes rather than anything else.

For instance, a few years ago, I think in 1923, the house passed an item in which words were introduced something to this effect, "for the use of manufacturers." It was stated at the time that these words were added simply to clarify the item, and certainly they sounded very innocent. The item applied to parts of machinery used in the cotton industry. The British manufacturer of cotton machinery naturally was forced to keep in Canada a depot of parts that might be required to promptly supply to machines that he had set up in Canada. On the other hand the American manufacturer in Boston-that was the chief centre-could ship in his parts overnight. Previously the tariff item had been 10 per cent in both cases. The amendment to which 1 refer had this effect, that the British manufacturer had to pay 15 per cent on the parts he sent to his depot here, while the American manufacturer paid only 10 per cent on the parts he sent in. As a matter of fact, the amendment was inserted at the instance of the American manufacturer, and he laughed at his British competitor and pointed out how he had put it over him. I think the discussion we have been having for the last hour and ten minutes is an illustration of the difficulty of that group government which my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) denounced so vociferously to 
the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) the other evening. We have had given us to-night an exhibition of government reclassification, but which is in reality an increase in the tariff on a number of items. No matter how much the attempt is made to hide it, that is what this amounts to. W'e find in the majority of these items that where there has been any change at all it has been a change to a higher tariff. That, without a doubt, is what has occurred. The Minister of Railways shakes his head, but in this group of items only one item in that group was free and that was after the minister came into the house to-night. The difficulty the government is in is very obvious. They have ministers like the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who are free traders, or say they are, and they have ministers like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) and the Minister of Finance himself, who are fairly good protectionists. And then they have the difficulty that when they travel out to the prairie provinces they tell those provinces that they are free traders; but when they travel through Quebec and Ontario they tell the people of those provinces that they are good protectionists, and they have to keep the balance in regard to their varying professions. Their action tonight reminded me a little of a Jewish friend of mine who is not a very good orthodox Jew. Of course he does not want to eat pork in public and whenever he does do so, he calls it chicken. Well, the ministers opposite me are in the same difficulty. They do not wish to call these changes in duty increased protection, so they call them a reclassification. That is what they are going to say when they are out in the prairie provinces. I bespeak sympathy on their behalf from the members from the prairie provinces, because they have great difficulties to overcome; but I rather think that from the standpoint of the country it would be far better for the Miinster of Finance to come right out and say that he is increasing protection, for that is what he is doing in some of these items. I venture to say that in the majority of cases he is hoodwinking the people; he is even trying to hoodwink parliament. I appeal to him to stop once in a while and give us a little chance. The Minister of Finance has this advantage, that he has had this matter before him for weeks while these items have only come before u*

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
quite recently, and it i3 only by chance in going through these items that we find out the real facts. I wish to congratulate the minister that in regard to many of these items he has pursued the course he has.
I am very glad to see him do it because I believe it will be productive of good to the whole country. I wish he would base his own budgets on the same principle, and I think if he did that he would do more for the country than he has been doing with his budgets for the last few years.

I may inform my hon. friends that I shall certainly go out and tell the people of the prairie provinces and the people of Canada generally regarding the reductions of duties in the consumers' items. My hon. friends opposite are accusing us of ruining the manufacturers. If we are doing what we are just now accused of doing, namely, raising the tariff, why all this three weeks of talk about ruining the industry? Surely the industry cannot be ruined if we have raised the consumers' items in the tariff. My hon. friend knows quitp well what the fact is. In the manufacturers' items there are adjustments, some upward and some downward, as a result of the examination which has been made; but when we come to the items which apply to the consuming public, it will be found that the adjustments are all downward.

Who purchases from the manufacturers, I should like to know? After listening to the remarks of the Minister of Railways, of all the yarns that exist in these tariff schedules I am sure there are none like those he tells the people when he is trying to get away with these changes.

Evidently those small companies are somewhat short on the influence end and the consumer in any event will be charged 5 per cent, 7i per cent or 10 per cent more for the cotton fabric manufactured out of those yarns.

Has the minister made any investigation to ascertain whether articles coming in from abroad really pay the tax, or whether the consumer pays it? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been in parliament
since 1908, and I have heard it argued on both sides as to who pays the customs duty. I admit frankly that I did not read all the evidence because I did not have time, and my hon. friend will not read it all; but I found from having run over the evidence and if my hon. friend reads part of it he also will find, about the same division of opinion before the tariff board as there is in this parliament as to who pays the customs duty.

I am not dealing with it
generally, because no matter how wide the knowledge of the minister and of his assistants may be, I do not think he can say in any general way that the consumer pays or that the foreign manufacturer and exporter pays the duty. But I do say that a careful investigation of any item, noting the sales in

Canada of the same grades, and the wholesale price in Canada as compared with the prices at which these same grades are sold for export to Canada, would divulge very, very important and relevant information, namely, whether the Canadian manufacturer is taking advantage of the tariff to exact undue prices in Canada. I do not pretend to be an expert, but I have given some attention to the matter, and I am firmly convinced that the Canadian manufacturer in three cases out of four is not making use of the tariff to exact from the Canadian consumer the prices which he might exact if he took full advantage of the tariff. I think that is the most important investigation that the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance could make. If the Finance minister on any occasion can show to me any item of the tariff which is being unduly taken advantage of to increase the price in Canada, then speaking for myself, I will vote with him either for an excise tax or a reduction of the customs tax which will prevent that abuse. Before these items are presented-the Finance minister himself may not have had time to read the evidence, I adimit that; I suppose in the administration of his department his time is taken up with many things other than this-but through the officials of his department the minister should be able to read that evidence and to ascertain its real purport, so that we may know with regard to these items whether, when increases are made, they are really necessary for the encouragement and protection of the Canadian industry concerned, or, when they are reduced, whether the reduction means or is likely to mean any reduction in price to the Canadian consumer. There is not an item on which, with the machinery the hon. gentleman and his colleagues command, they could not ascertain and present a fair analysis of these facts. I believe we on this side of the house are just as serious as the hon. minister himself in our opposition to abuse of the tariff for the purpose of profiteering,and therefore when reductions are made we wish to know whether the .tariff as it stands is being made use of for that purpose, or whether it simply stands as an element of protection against foreign competition and against the foreign dumping to which this market is subject.

I may repeat that my hon.
friend will find some evidence in the reports tabled indicating the prices in the different countries and the cost of production. I have not very much objection to the statement of my hon. friend. He has convinced me of something that I had in my own mind, and I think he will agree with me, that if the Canadian manufacturers of textiles and cottons have not been taking full advantage of the tariff, the reductions we have made will not do them any harm.

I submit that they will do them harm, and do the great bulk of the consuming population in Canada no good. In order to ascertain the facte as far as I could, I went to a manufacturer-I am not going into details as to names and all that-and his reply was that he was prepared to show me that his factory or factories had never taken advantage of the tariff in all these years, except on two or three occasions when dumping was attempted against them; or the dumping may have been due to depreciation of foreign currency, which amounts to exactly the same thing. But, he said, if you do not give us protection against the dumping during two or three months of the year by the foreign producer with a surplus on hand in his own market which he will put into the Canadian market as any price, giving a temporary price advantage for a few days or weeks in the Canadian market-if you do not protect us against that, we are bound for our own protection to take full advantage of the reduced tariff in order that we may make up during the nine or ten months of the year the loss which we sustain due to the large dumping which takes place in those two or three months. I am convinced that the person talking to me wias absolutely sincere: as a matter of fact, I have reason to believe he is a supporter of the hon. gentleman and of his party. But I was talking to him as a serious man in order that I might get a fair understanding of the case of the manufacturer, and I think it is due to us as members of this house that we should have the data placed before us. If the hon. gentleman has not had time in the weeks and months-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have placed the evidence on the table.

I know it is on the table, and I make no reflection on the minister because I know that as head of the Finance department it is absolutely impossible for him to read it. But he has ample assistance; he has eyes to read for him and brains to think for him, and how can I as a private
member of this house digest a typewritten document of this extent which is placed on the table only two or three weeks ago? It is absolutely impossible for me to study it. Before this budget was brought down, before it was attempted, a statement ought to have been laid before us with regard to these more important items which would enable us to elucidate the facts and to ascertain whether the manufacturers affected are abusing the tariff for their own profiteering, or whether this action is really necessary to protect them against foreign dumping and foreign currency depreciation at a time when they are not using the tariff for any improper purposes 'but are giving the consumer during nine to eleven months of the year the full advantage that can be given him in the price of the staple products that are placed on this market.
Mr. 'SPEARMAN: Mr. Chairman, the question raised by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George whether a reduction in duty actually reduces the cost of the article to the consumer, is rather important. One thing, however, that may throw some light upon the subject is the obvious anxiety of many manufacturers to have their imports of raw materials placed upon the free list. It is evident that when they in their turn become importers, they believe, whether rightly or wrongly, that the reduction of the duty does reduce the cost of the article.

The point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) is, as has been intimated, a very important one indeed. The charge is very commonly made that one reason why we should not have a protective tariff at all is that the Canadian manufacturer takes full advantage of the duty imposed, and therefore the consumer must pay that duty in addition to the normal price of the manufactured article. When this subject was under discussion about three years ago .1 went to several of our representative industries and asked then to give me the privilege of examining their cost records and other books to ascertain for myself whether or not such a practice was being carried on. They were important firms, and were kind enough to give me free access to the information that I desired. I found on examination of the cost sheets and books of, I think, six or seven firms that the duty never entered into their process of price fixing. The factors entering into it, of course, are overhead, rentals, cost of material, wages, and so on-the usual charges against the manufactured article. Then a certain profit was charged according to the

class of goods manufactured, for instance, with a boot and shoe factory it was 7i per cent, with another concern it was 5 per cent, with another 11 per cent; but in no instance did the manufacturer take into consideration the tariff duty in fixing the price of his commodity. And that is exactly what ought to be done in all these cases. There should be no inclusion of the amount of protection in fixing the price of the commodity manufactured. I am citing this-and I am very glad the hon. member brought the question to the attention of the committee-because I think a very excellent service could be rendered to the public in the first instance, and to the honest manufacturer and dealer in the second, if the tariff advisory board would make it a point to examine the records of companies with this point in view. For instance, if a company appeared before them either to defend a proposed reduction or to ask for an increase of duty, and it was found that such company took full advantage of the tariff schedules, then I say it would deserve very little consideration, if any. As a matter of fact I think the tariff advisory board should make a finding according to the facts. The result would be that such concerns or groups of industries as abuse the privilege of the tariff could be disciplined either by a reduction of the tariff or the imposition of an excise tax. That is the proper way to deal with it. On the other hand the honest Canadian industrialist, carrying on his business according tb the sound and welll known principles of economics, is entitled from this country to a fair deal and reasonable tariff protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who in the last analysis would pay that excise tax?

The manufacturer or group of industries offending. After all, our industries are pretty well organized to-day. For instance, we have the automobile industry, the cotton industry, the woollen industry all grouped; in fact all the major industries are grouped. If it were found that, say, the cotton industry was abusing the privileges of the tariff by adding the full amount of the duty to their commodity price, then the imposition of the excise tax would be on the manufacturers in that industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would not they pass it on to the consumer?

Not necessarily at all.
That when you impose a tax it alone goes to the consumer is the most utter fallacy that can

be maintained. Rent goes to the consumer, also insurance, in fact anything that is a charge against the cost of the material in the course of its manufacture goes to the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am interested in this, and as my hon. friend has made a study of the subject he may be able to clear up the point. Does he argue that we should place an excise tax upon a domestic manufacturer and allow imports to come in without that excise tax?

Not at all. If a group of industries are found to be abusing the privileges of the tariff, that is, adding the full amount of duty when it is not necessary for their welfare, then I say impose an excise tax, or, if you prefer, lower the duty-either one or the other. I am inclined to think that the best way would be to impose an excise tax, because then the exchequer would be benefited.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But let us clear this up so that it will go out right to the country. Then the policy would be to impose an excise tax only on the domestic manufacturer?
No, the minister cannot corner me in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not trying to.

It appears to me that he is. The point I am making is this. If a Canadian industry having a protection, we will say, of 15 per cent is able to manufacture its article just as cheaply as it is manufactured abroad, and the industry be healthy, we will say that 10 per cent is a fair profit; but the manufacturer adds 15 per cent, thus abusing the privileges of the tariff. Then I say, either reduce the tariff to 10 per cent, or impose an excise tax of 5 per cent, whichever you think will more effectively cure the abuse. That is where the tariff advisory board W'ould function. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can follow my hon. friend when he urges for a reduction of the tariff; but when he favours putting an excise tax not only on the domestic but on the imported article, I do not understand how he would change the price.

I did not say that. I want to be clear on this; I do not want it to be hurled at me later that I made a statement which as a matter of fact I did not make. Mark you, where an industry is acting fairly with the Canadian public nothing should be done. Let us make that clear,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

But where an industry is abusing its tariff protection, taking full advantage of the duty, although it does not need it, then I say impose upon that industry an excise tax or reduce the tariff.
Mr. Chairman-

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. It is well understood in this house that an hon. member may discuss almost anything during the budget debate. The budget debate is concluded, and I do not know that we have any rule to permit a member discussing everything under the sun when a tariff item is under consideration by the committee. I did not wish to call my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) to order because he had not an opportunity of speaking on the budget, but I do think that this house has wandered far from the rules both during the budget debate and in committee. Hon. members should stick to the item under discussion or we shall never get through.
The point is well taken, and I would ask the committee to confine itself more closely to the subject under discussion, namely, item 522.

I have been dealing with
item 522 right straight along. My point is that before any reduction is made in that item we should have a specific comparison of prices abroad, either in England or in the United States, with the prices which are exacted in Canada. When t'he Minister of Finance says an excise tax would not prevent abuse and undue profits, I tell him that such a tax placed on Canadian production would take away undue profits. And the excise tax upon the foreign product has no relation to the question in dealing with cotton yarn. It has no relation to it whatsoever, because if the tariff is so high as to enable the domestic manufacturer to take undue advantage of it and to profiteer on his sales, then it is so high that no excise tax imposed upon the foreign exporter into Canada will help the situation at all. If we look into the facts and find a factory or a group of factories unduly profiteering in cotton yarns then there is intelligence enough in the Finance department as well as in the Department of National Revenue to ascertain where a reduction in the duty is necessary, or whether the imposition of a form of excise tax, taking away the undue profits made by that factory or group of factories, would result to the advantage of the Canadian consumer. You cannot convince me that a factory or group of factories manufacturing cotton yams will indulge unduly in profiteering except to secure a profit to that factory or group of factories. According to my suggestion you take away the excess profit and every incentive to deal unfairly and unjustly with the Canadian consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend a moment ago inquired as to investigating costs in other countries. I find this memorandum from the board to the minister:
Almost every reference to the board has contained statements regarding conditions in foreign countries, and especially wages and labour costs. In many instances the sources of information thus presented have not been clearly defined, in others the information furnished has not been up to date. Not infrequently both applicants and opponents have contended that the duty of determining conditions at the origin of export fell upon the board. Unfortunately the board has had neither the time nor the financial resources for conducting detailed investigations abroad in all the matters referred to it, and it must be admitted, in several of the applications, has not yet been able to secure satisfying information.
I take it, therefore, that the board has that question under consideration. I do not wish to precipitate a longer debate, but in one particular case-I am not saying that it was sound tactics-one of the textile industries of another country came voluntarily before the board and presented evidence as to costs in that country. My hon. friends opposite have found much fault with that procedure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not with their presentation as to wages, but with their observations respecting the applications themselves and the examination of witnesses, which is an entirely different thing. I have taken the trouble to read carefully what they did say and if the minister will do the same he will see the pertinence of my remarks in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I admit that it was not the
best of manners.

The tariff board in the
United States has a number of experts who make investigations abroad regarding prices, costs of production and so forth, so that they have, in respect of any tariff item, all the material which I am now suggesting should be available to the Minister of Finance. It seems to me that, so far as production in foreign countries is concerned, advantage might be taken to a certain extent of such researches. In competition between us and the United States I consider it the duty of the tariff board to make these investigations by expert assistance. Means should be placed at the disposal of the board for this

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We should bear in mind also the fact that our membership in the League of Nations gives us access to that large body of information, to which I ventured to refer the other day, regarding wages. The International Labour Bureau, maintained in connection with the league, makes available for us all that information with respect to wages and the relation of wages in foreign countries to our own. The trade commissioners are also in a position to furnish the same information. The index figure, according to an article in the National Magazine of last month in connection with British industry, showed that when it was 100 in England it was 153 in Ottawa and 175 in Philadelphia. The various countries in the world were given, and especially low were the figures in some of the Balkan states and in Belgium. I cannot see why the tariff board should not avail itself of information thus secured by the International Labour Bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they do use such information to a considerable extent.

I understand that the
minister has put on record some figures regarding the production of various yams in Canada.

to say whether item 522, cotton yams, not exceeding 20's single, 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent, constitutes an increase or a reduction in the tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have been discussing the items generally. I do not know whether my hon. friend wants to get on the record at this late hour all the facts bearing on the matter. In this particular item alone there is an increase.

There is an increase in
item 522?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but taking them altogether there is a very considerable decrease.

I thought we would take
them one at a time. The minister has referred to the assistance he received from the tariff board, which it was stated earlier in the evening was a fact-finding body. It is advisory, apparently, in connection with the fixing of the tariff schedules.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I should be very glad if
the minister could recollect those recommendations made by the tariff board, not in writing but at those conferences of which he told us, which extended into the late hours of the night. What was the basis upon which the tariff board made a recommendation for the increase of any duty? Was it on the basis of taking care of or protecting, if you like, the particular industry under discussion? If so, was that communicated to the minister and was it used by him in arriving at the schedule rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in any particular industry. If my hon. friend will say the industries throughout Canada I will repeat what I said this afternoon, that in the case of some industries, some particular items, the government did not go as far as the tariff board thought they might go. The tariff board, having heard all the evidence both from the manufacturers and from the other side, thought there might be an increase in some cases, but the government determined differently.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because that was not the business of the tariff board.

I am afraid I am not quite
answered yet. I am anxious to know the principle upon which advice was given by the tariff board. In making their recommendations or reports, whatever you call them, did they indicate that they were proceeding on the principle of protecting industry generally? Did they indicate that some particular industry required for its protection from competition from abroad, or for various reasons, some increase in the tariff schedule, or is the report or advice of the tariff board a hit and miss affair? Do they say, "We think this industry can stand a little and this other industry cannot stand it so well"? If there is no principle at all behind the recommendations of that board, what possible system have the government in arriving at a definite figure?

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The system of common sense, as far as we understand it; the same system hon. members opposite would follow if they had the responsibility of office. The idea is to do what we believe is in the best general interests of the people of Canada.

All I can say to that statement is that I am very grateful for the implied compliment that because we did it it is right, but the point I am making in regard to this or any other item is this: If you are going on the advice of the tariff board, that advice to be valid and worth acting upon must be founded on some principle, otherwise it is a hit and miss affair. In the hands of a government which wanted to make use of it the tariff could be very readily used, under these circumstances, as an instrument for imposing upon industries and getting money from them, if you will. I am not suggesting for a moment that that has been done, but the tariff board, constituted with no definite principles upon which to make these recommendations, can be more readily made a toll gate than a tariff board. I am not speaking of the personnel now. So I say that the temptation to any government of having an instrument such as this ready to its hand is too strong, unless the recommendations of that instrument are to be based upon some definite principle. I should like to know if they have been so based.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not like these insinuations, which come up from time to time, that the tariff board might 'be a toll gate. If my hon. friend advances that argument he might as well say that the government he supported when they were in office carried on a toll gate, and I do not believe they did. They used their best judgment at the time.

No, I particularly said that
I was not speaking of the personnel of the tariff board or of the government at all. I am only speaking of the uselessness of a tariff board which is constituted with no definite principle. A tariff board was set up in India and another in the United States; I prefer to speak of the one set up in India, which was constituted on the definite principle of protection as the guide to the recommendations they should make. They knew where they were; they knew what facts they wanted to get and the government had a finding based on some policy upon which to act. Now I say that as long as our tariff board is not properly constituted in that regard, there is the danger that it may be made just what I have indicated. I am making no insinuations; at the moment I am just trying to discuss the functions of the tariff board which brought in a report favouring an increase of the duty on this particular item 522.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say they advocated it in this particular item; I do not recall whether or not they did, but I think I have caught my hon. friend's point now. He says that the United States board received instructions and was created as a method of protection. Am I right in that?
The board in India.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our board is different; it is a fact-finding body. In this large country there is a wide difference of opinion, some people believe in absolute free trade, at least one of whom sits over yonder. Other gentlemen are here, representing different constituencies, who advocate higher tariff. We have had two or three elections in this country on the tariff issue alone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: All of them, you say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps all of them. We
created the tariff board so that those who advocated a higher tariff and those who advocated a lower tariff could go before that board and submit to it all the facts they could produce in support of their position. The board reports to the government, and the government must take the responsibility for the policy adopted.
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance one question. He says the tariff board is a fact finding body. H that is so we should have a report of the facts which have been found.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
